purpose: Pralsetinib is used to treat certain types of lung cancer and thyroid cancer that have a specific gene change called a RET mutation or RET fusion. It works best when your doctor has tested your tumor and confirmed this specific gene change is present. It is a targeted therapy, meaning it goes after a specific abnormal signal driving your cancer.
how_it_works: Inside some cancer cells, a gene called RET gets altered and sends out constant signals telling the cancer cells to grow and spread out of control. Pralsetinib works by blocking that faulty RET signal, like turning off a stuck switch. Without that signal, the cancer cells have a much harder time growing and surviving.
common_side_effects: Feeling tired or weak, constipation, muscle or joint pain, high blood pressure, swelling in the hands or feet, decreased appetite, low levels of certain blood cells (like white blood cells and platelets), fever, and changes in liver or kidney lab values.
warnings: Pralsetinib can cause serious lung problems (like inflammation in the lungs), high blood pressure that needs to be monitored and treated, liver problems, and bleeding. It can also cause harm to an unborn baby, so both men and women should use effective birth control during treatment and for a period after stopping. Tell your doctor right away if you have new or worsening shortness of breath, cough, fever, unusual bleeding, or yellowing of the skin or eyes. It may also interact with other medications, so always share your full medication list with your care team.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 400 mg (four 100 mg capsules) taken by mouth once a day on an empty stomach — meaning you should not eat for at least 2 hours before and at least 1 hour after taking it. Take it at the same time each day and swallow the capsules whole. If you miss a dose and it has been more than 6 hours, skip the missed dose and take your next dose as scheduled.
